title: Grids (Electricity 2026 chapter)
verification: full page read 2026-11-02.
relevance: The current IEA bottleneck account: over 2,500 GW of renewable, large-load and storage projects are stalled in grid queues worldwide. Annual grid investment needs to increase by approximately 50 percent by 2030 from today's USD 400 billion, alongside a scale-up in grid supply chains. Planning, permitting and completing new grid infrastructure takes 5 to 15 years, against 1 to 5 years for renewables projects, 1 to 3 years for data centres and 1 to 2 years for EV charging infrastructure, and prices for key grid components have nearly doubled over the past five years. Grid-enhancing technologies alone (dynamic line rating, dynamic transformer rating, advanced power flow control, topology optimisation, storage as a transmission asset, plus reconductoring and voltage uprating) could unlock 450 to 700 GW, with the caveat that benefits cannot be stacked additively because several solutions address the same constraints. The chapter also includes a section on the synchronisation of the Baltic power system in February 2025, summarised here only as included, not in detail.

title: Energy and AI, Box 5.4: Water use by data centres
authors: Thomas Spencer and Siddharth Singh (lead authors)
verification: Box 5.4 page read 2026-11-02; rest of report left unread.
relevance: The global water baseline for AI infrastructure. Global data centre water consumption is around 560 billion litres per year (2023), rising to around 1,200 billion litres per year in 2030 in the Base Case. About two thirds of 2023 consumption comes from primary energy supply and electricity generation, one quarter from direct cooling, and the remainder from semiconductor and microchip manufacturing. An average 100 MW hyperscale data centre in the US consumes around 2 million litres per day in total, equivalent to about 6,500 households, with over 60 percent indirect. Solar PV and wind use one hundredth of the water of fossil sources or less. Almost 90 percent of manufacturing-stage water consumption is ultrapure water production, and chip manufacturing water consumption grows more than 50 percent from 2023 to around 70 billion litres in 2030. In Chinese Taipei, semiconductor manufacturers faced water restrictions during the 2021 drought. Around half of 2030 consumption is in Asia Pacific countries, where warm humid climates make cooling more water intensive. Microsoft's direct-cooling WUE for Asia Pacific was 1.65 L/kWh, more than three times its global average of around 0.5 L/kWh (Microsoft, 2022). The Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact targets WUE below 0.4 L/kWh by 2040, and the US average WUE was estimated at 0.36 L/kWh for 2023. Direct liquid cooling and immersion cooling can reduce direct water consumption significantly. AWS and Google have pledged to be water positive by 2030. Withdrawals are total water withdrawn, consumption is the portion not returned to the source. This record is a distinct Box 5.4 entry; the catalogue already has a separate iea-energy-and-ai record for the report as a whole, at a different URL.

Data centres consume water three ways, from most to least direct: cooling systems, the electricity supply (gas and nuclear stations evaporate water), and semiconductor chip manufacturing (processed water to rinse wafers). The IEA estimate of global data centre water consumption around 560 billion litres per year rising to around 1,200 billion litres per year by 2030 is set against UK non-household water use of around 1,000 billion litres per year in 2024 to 2025. Cooling table figures: chilled-water CRAH up to 25 million litres per MW per year, indirect free air cooling about 8 million litres per MW per year, evaporative or adiabatic about 1 to 8 million litres per MW per year depending on climate and method, direct free air near zero. title: Thirsty Data and the Lone Star State: The Impact of Data Center Growth on Texas' Water Supply
galaxy_topics: infrastructure/water, infrastructure/centres, infrastructure/electricity, politics/national, governance/rules, environment/resources
verification: executive summary read 2026-11-02; body chapters left unread.
relevance: The Texas case: where data centre water demand meets a state water plan that does not count it. As of September 2025 Texas has more than 400 data centre facilities (Baxtel count 464) concentrated in five regions (Dallas/Fort Worth 197, Houston 48, San Antonio 60, Austin 53, West Texas 59), requiring approximately 9,567 MW. Between direct on-site cooling and indirect electricity generation, existing Texas data centres consume approximately 25 billion gallons of water in 2025 (77 thousand acre-feet), 0.4 percent of total state water use. If growth projections hold, demand could rise to 29 to 161 billion gallons by 2030 (0.5 to 2.7 percent of annual state use). ERCOT estimates data centres could require 22,175 to 77,965 MW by 2030. The Texas State Water Plan does not include projected data centre demand growth, and Texas has no guidelines or requirements to address large water demands through efficiency, conservation or alternative supplies. Recommendations include requiring and releasing better electricity and water demand data, including large water demand uses in water planning, groundwater regulation reform, incentivising or requiring water reuse or conservation and offsets in the same river basin or aquifer, and public-private supply solutions.

title: Water Use and Community Trust: Key Components of Data Centers' Social License to Operate
verification: executive summary read 2026-11-02 plus introduction and key takeaways; body left unread.
relevance: The social licence record: why water becomes a siting constraint even when national volumes look small. While national-level water use from data centres remains relatively modest, localised impacts combined with limited transparency are driving rising community opposition and creating material risks to project development. Community acceptance is shaped less by absolute water volumes and more by perceptions of fairness, transparency, and long-term resource sustainability. Cooling technology choices involve unavoidable tradeoffs: water-efficient systems typically increase energy demand, while energy-efficient systems decrease direct water consumption but increase indirect water consumption. Indirect water use linked to thermoelectric power generation can exceed direct cooling water use by a factor of three (Siddik et al., 2021). An estimated 84 percent of data centre water consumption is attributable to hyperscale facilities, and Bloomberg News reports approximately two-thirds of data centers built or in development since 2022 are located in regions experiencing high levels of water stress (Bloomberg, 2025). Regulatory compliance alone is insufficient to secure community trust; projects that proactively engage stakeholders, adopt non-potable water strategies, and provide transparent, locally relevant information are more likely to achieve a durable social license to operate. The paper concludes that proactive water stewardship, including improved disclosure and early, meaningful community engagement, is essential not only for environmental performance but also for securing a durable social license to operate.
